#Agriculture: The @UNFAO Food Price Index averaged 136 points in September, reaching a 4½-year high and rising 5.8% year-on-year. The increase was driven primarily by strong gains in sugar (+6.1%) and cereals (+5.1%), with vegetable oils (+0.9%) also contributing. Meat prices (-1.1%) were the only major component to decline last month, while dairy prices were broadly unchanged.

Highlights from the report: 
The FAO Cereal Price Index rose sharply in September, driven by tightening supply and growing logistical risks. Wheat prices were supported by Black Sea export constraints, which pushed buyers towards alternative origins, as well as dry weather ahead of North American winter wheat planting. Maize also strengthened as disappointing US yields, reduced Brazilian export availability and Black Sea disruptions tightened the supply outlook. Elevated fuel, fertiliser and freight costs linked to uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz added further support, particularly for crops with biofuel exposure. Rice prices edged higher on weather concerns and seasonally tighter supplies.

The FAO Vegetable Oil Price Index rose modestly, led by palm oil, where strong import demand and concerns about dry weather affecting Southeast Asian production outweighed weakness elsewhere. Sunflower oil declined on expectations of ample Black Sea supplies, although logistical constraints limited the downside. Soy oil remained supported by robust biofuel demand.

The FAO Meat Price Index declined as ample supplies weighed on poultry and pork. Brazilian poultry exports faced softer EU demand following new import requirements, while increased pig meat availability across major producing regions pressured prices. Beef and sheep meat prices were broadly stable, with regional differences reflecting shifts in demand, trade policy and currency movements.

The FAO Dairy Price Index was broadly unchanged. Strong Asian demand and limited prompt availability supported milk powder prices, while cheese weakened amid softer European demand, strong US export competition and rising seasonal supply from Oceania. Butter was little changed, with tighter European milkfat availability offsetting weaker prices elsewhere.

The FAO Sugar Price Index rose strongly as the market priced a tighter global supply outlook. Smaller EU beet acreage and adverse weather, weaker production prospects in Thailand, concerns about India's crop amid below-normal rainfall and developing El Niño conditions, and harvest disruptions caused by heavy rain in Brazil all contributed to the increase.

The energy complex trades lower, led by gasoil (-4.7%) and ULSD (-3.3%), as the US pressures France and Germany to release emergency diesel stocks or potentially face a US diesel export ban. France has reportedly proposed releasing 50 million barrels of European diesel and 50 million barrels of crude across IEA members, conditional on Washington refraining from unilateral export restrictions, with G7 leaders potentially discussing next steps later today (Reuters).

The developments once again highlight that the main stress in energy markets has shifted from crude availability to refined products. Middle East crude flows are recovering, but reduced refinery capacity and output across the Middle East and Russia, together with China cancelling oil-product export cargoes to bolster domestic supply, continue to constrain global fuel availability and keep prices elevated.

The Bloomberg chart shows gasoil (white) and ULSD (blue) priced in USD per barrel both falling to one-month lows on this development.

RBOB gasoline leads this week’s performance table, up 5.8%, after the EIA reported a further decline in nationwide inventories to their lowest since November 2014. Distillate stocks also fell to their lowest seasonal level on record, with product tightness partly reflecting a seasonal and temporary drop in refinery activity, as crude runs fell by 1 mb/d to a five-month low. Meanwhile, US crude exports slowed to 3.6 mb/d as more Middle Eastern barrels were heading for the global market, while domestic production climbed to another record at 13.96 mb/d.
Ironically, Saudi Arabia now has more export capacity available (when combining both coasts) than it did prior to the war. Meanwhile, Iran is shipping out zero bpd.

During this conflict, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the UAE have (on average) exported 26% fewer barrels of crude oil than they did during the same period last year, while the average price per barrel has risen 44% this year.
